messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Social Worker
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men, Known People: Related people, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Helena Novak is an 80-year-old social worker who came to treatment after years of trying to manage alone the aftermath of a violent relationship in late life. She had been living with a man she trusted when the abuse escalated into episodes of physical assault behind closed doors in her apartment. What remains with her is not a smooth story but a set of brutal images: his face changing as he stepped toward her, the sudden movement of his arm, the sound of a door thrown open and then slammed hard enough to shake the frame, her own body bracing before she could think. Even now, when she tries to describe what happened, she loses the sequence. She says it comes back as separate pictures rather than a continuous memory, and when those pictures break through she is flooded less with fear than with a heavy, overwhelming grief for the woman she had been before she let him into her life.

In the months after she left him, Helena found that certain moments in ordinary life carried the force of the assault. A male colleague lingering after a meeting, being alone in her office with a male client, a relative of a family she was serving stepping too close in a doorway, or simply hearing a door open sharply in the corridor could pull up one of those picture-like fragments. The trigger and the memory arrived together: the door sound became his entrance, the presence of a man became the instant before impact. Each time, the broken nature of the recollection seemed to confirm something corrosive to her about what had happened. She had come to believe that whatever rules she once trusted about decency, safety, and knowing people were gone, and that people, especially men, could not be trusted even when they were familiar or connected to someone she knew. At her lowest moments after these reminders, she also felt sullied by the abuse, as if something dirty had been left on her.

Those meanings began to organize her days. Because she was certain the world no longer worked by any safe or understandable rules, Helena started thinking over and over about why this had happened to her, searching for an explanation that would restore some order and never finding one. She tried just as hard to get rid of the memories entirely, cutting off thoughts the moment they rose, refusing conversations that might bring them up, and steering herself away from the evening routines and quiet hours that tended to end in nightmares. The more contaminated and mistrustful she felt, the more necessary these efforts seemed to her; avoiding dreams, erasing the memory, and turning the event over in her mind were all attempts to contain what she believed the abuse had revealed.

Her body, meanwhile, behaved as if danger were still close. Helena now scans for exits as soon as she enters any room or building. In the agency where she still works part-time, she chooses chairs with a clear line to the door and notices every man who comes into the waiting area before she can attend to the conversation in front of her. She is superalert, watchful, and she sleeps badly, often lying awake listening for sounds in the hallway. This constant state of readiness fits with her conviction that people cannot be trusted; if no place is truly safe, then she must stay on guard. But the vigilance has also made her life smaller. Because she is already keyed up by bedtime and dreads what the night might bring, she avoids the times and situations that she associates with dreaming, staying up with the television on or keeping herself busy until exhaustion overtakes her.

Over time these habits have tightened around the triggers themselves. Her efforts to push away the memory seem to make door sounds more potent, and the men she encounters in the ordinary course of social work feel increasingly charged before they have done anything at all. She notices whether an office door is closed, how close a male client sits, whether a husband or brother accompanies a family member; her watchfulness finds the very cues she fears. When a reminder does break through, the memory is again only a few shattering images, and their incompleteness leaves room for more brooding about why this happened and what it says about the world. The repeated attempts to blot it out have not restored her trust; if anything, they have deepened her sense that the abuse permanently changed her and left her unclean. The loss is practical as well as emotional. She has started limiting home visits if a man might be present and asks colleagues to swap certain cases, something she never did before and finds humiliating after a lifetime of competent work.

What finally brought Helena in was an incident at work when a door slammed in the corridor just as she was alone with the adult son of a client. She froze, immediately searched for the exit, and later sat in her car unable to stop crying. She said she was frightened that her world was shrinking to hallways, doors, and men to avoid, and that if she could not sleep or trust her own mind, she might have to give up the work that still gives her purpose. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not to forget what happened but to stop living as though it is still about to happen again.
